intro_en: The Israel National Trail crosses the low Shephelah (Judean foothills), through gentle hills, vineyards, groves and fields.
character_en: Gentle, with easy ascents and descents; mostly exposed to the sun, and partly passing through woodland.
transport_en: The turnoff to Kibbutz Beit Guvrin. The turnoff to Moshav Ahuzam, a little north of Tel Keshet.
pois_en: Tel Lachish – a large and important biblical site right beside the trail. Tel Keshet.
important_en: As in all the hills of the Shephelah, it is important to walk only on clear paths because of the risk of falling into open pits.
Take care not to drink from the taps and not to enter the cultivated plots. There is a concern about toxic pesticides and fertilizers.
Tel Lachish is in the process of being prepared for opening as a national park with an entrance fee (as of November 2021).
There is a minimarket at Moshav Lachish for stocking up.
description_en:
We leave the gas station toward the nearby junction and carefully cross Road 38. Beyond the safety barrier, the trail climbs to the right to the high ground above the road. A short walk up the hill brings us to "the Villa" – the remains of a two-story Arab building from a village destroyed during the War of Independence.
The trail continues south from the other side of the building and comes out into open country. After about an hour's walk along the edge of the fields on a dirt road, we reach vineyards that herald the farmland of Moshav Lachish.
After another half hour or so of walking beside the vineyards we reach the Lachish–Amatzia road. In the past traffic on this road was sparse, but today it is busy – so take care when crossing. To the east several communities have been established, among them Eliav, Neta and Bnei Dekalim, and existing communities have been expanded. After the disengagement from the Gaza Strip the population of the area grew significantly.
We proceed south on a dirt road and pass below Tel Lachish – a large and important archaeological mound. Among the discoveries made there: the "Lachish Letters" – more than 20 letters on potsherds from the end of the First Temple period. We continue on the dirt road at the foot of the tel, and after a short walk pass vineyards on the left. At this point we can stray a little from the trail and take in the tel's remarkable story. A good spot to stop is after a short climb to the right, to the saddle inside the pine grove. Among the stories linked to the tel: the siege of Lachish by the Assyrian king Sennacherib some 2,700 years ago, which is even mentioned in the Bible. A depiction of the siege appears on a relief found in Nineveh, and there is evidence of it at the tel too. On the southern slope of the tel, toward the saddle, the remains of the siege ramp can be seen.
On the southern side of the tel there is a water tap and a picnic area, and about half a km from there – a minimarket at Moshav Lachish.
We return to the trail, to the dirt road at the edge of the vineyards, and continue south. We walk between the vineyards for about half an hour, and a little after the southern vineyards of Moshav Lachish the trail turns west. Beside the turn is a grove of eucalyptus trees – a possible spot for a rest stop.
We walk west toward Road 6, with expanses of fields on the left. Before Road 6 we pass through two groves – which offer shaded rest spots. To the west the expanses of the southern coastal plain around Ashkelon come into view, and in front of them the traffic on Road 6.
At the point where the trail reaches the fence that bounds the highway zone, it turns south (left) and continues along the fence, descending toward the channel of Nahal Adorayim – a large tributary of Nahal Shikma that originates in the Hebron area. We follow the streambed west, in its direction of flow toward the sea. We cross Road 6 and the Be'er Sheva–Kiryat Gat railway line beneath the bridges built over the channel.
The trail continues with the streambed between the railway line and Road 40. Road 40 too is crossed beneath the bridge over the stream channel. On the other side of the bridge a lone palm tree juts up; beyond it is Tel Keshet, and here the segment ends.
To reach a point where a vehicle can pick us up, there are 2 options: continue north along Road 40 to the entrance to Moshav Ahuzam, or a longer walk south to the entrance to Philip Farm (Havat Philip).
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, trail-marking coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
